lessons.title: Plot and Structure: A Tale Across Two Countries

before.content_html:
Two Worlds, One Stage

The Great Wave by Francis Turnly spans almost a quarter of a century — from 1979 to 2003 — across two nations that share a coastline but almost nothing else. The structural challenge Turnly sets himself is formidable: how do you tell a story in which two families live through the same event from opposite sides of a border, across two decades, without ever fully knowing the same facts? His answer is a rigorously disciplined cross-cutting structure that forces the audience into the uncomfortable position of knowing more than any single character ever does.

The play is structured in two acts. The first act establishes the catastrophic event at its centre — the abduction of Hanako from the coast of Japan by North Korean agents during a storm in 1979 — and then splits into its two parallel lines: Hanako in North Korea, and her family in Japan. The second act moves deeper into adulthood, into diplomacy and silence, and towards the Pyongyang Declaration of 2002, which acknowledged for the first time that such abductions had taken place. By choosing this two-act, twin-timeline structure, Turnly gives the audience a form that mirrors its content: separation, parallel endurance, and the impossibility of reunion that looks easy from the outside.

Key Fact

The play spans 1979 to 2003 across two parallel storylines: Hanako in North Korea (abducted as a teenager) and her family in Japan (searching, grieving, advocating). The twin timelines converge emotionally but almost never physically.

The Opening Beach Scene

The play opens in a storm. Two teenage sisters — Hanako and Reiko — are on the coast of Japan, arguing. Turnly’s stage directions foreground the sea: its sound, its scale, its menace. This is the last time we will see both sisters together in the same present moment for the rest of the play. For a director, the staging of this scene is one of the most consequential choices in the whole production. Working in an in-the-round configuration, the sea becomes a surround-sound presence rather than a painted flat: waves can come from all directions, making the audience feel the disorientation of the storm. In a more traditional proscenium arch configuration, the beach might be signalled by a raked stage, a strip of projected surf at the back, and a soundscape of crashing water that gradually overwhelms the sisters’ voices.

As a performer playing Reiko in this opening moment, the choices you make about posture and proximity signal the relationship before a word is spoken. Place Reiko upstage of Hanako and have her turn away as Hanako tries to speak — the physical distance communicates the argument’s emotional temperature before either line is delivered. As a sound designer, you might begin with a low, continuous underscore of distant waves, then swell the volume as the sisters’ argument reaches its peak, so that the sea literally drowns their voices at the moment of separation — a design choice that carries the controlling metaphor of the title into the audience’s ears.

Cross-cutting means the play shifts between its two storylines in alternating scenes rather than completing one before starting the other. In The Great Wave, Turnly cuts from Hanako’s captivity in North Korea to the Hashimoto family in Japan and back again, sometimes within the same act. This structure creates dramatic irony — the audience knows Hanako is alive while her family does not — and it holds both truths simultaneously rather than letting the audience forget either one.

For a director, these transitions need a clear lighting state change at each cross-cut. A common approach is a sudden blackout followed immediately by a new state — colder in North Korea, warmer in Japan — so the audience registers the geography shift through temperature and colour before any dialogue confirms it. The costume of the performers can reinforce this: subdued utility fabrics and muted earth tones in the DPRK sequences; softer domestic textures and layered clothing in the Japanese family sequences.

Time Leaps and the Ageing Body

Because the play moves across more than two decades, the performers playing Hanako and her family must communicate ageing without realistic prosthetics. Turnly’s stage directions indicate time leaps through lighting changes, sound shifts and costume alteration. A blocking strategy commonly used to communicate ageing is to give a character a progressively reduced range of movement as years accumulate — a youthful Hanako who crosses the stage in a few quick strides becomes, a decade later, a figure who moves in deliberate, contained steps, her energy disciplined by years of captivity. This is not naturalistic ageing — it is a theatrical shorthand that makes the passage of time legible in the performer’s body.

For the audience, this physical storytelling across time is more powerful than any chronological caption could be. When Etsuko, the mother, is seen in two scenes separated by a decade, a lighting designer might shift from a warmer, amber-tinted state in the earlier scene to a cooler, lower-intensity wash in the later one — signalling not just time but emotional weathering. A gobo patterned to suggest window bars or a lattice might appear in the North Korean scenes to suggest confinement without building a cell.

Key Fact

Turnly signals time leaps through lighting state changes, costume alterations and sound cues rather than captions or narration. This places the burden of storytelling on design rather than exposition, which gives the audience an active interpretive role.

Epic Structure and Documentary Roots

The structure of The Great Wave belongs to the tradition of documentary theatre — a tradition associated with the Tricycle Theatre (now the Kiln Theatre) in Kilburn, where the play premiered in 2018 under director Indhu Rubasingham before transferring to the National Theatre’s Dorfman stage. Documentary theatre typically presents itself as evidence rather than fiction; even though The Great Wave has invented characters, its structural discipline — the dual timeline, the diplomatic scenes, the precision of its historical markers (1979, 1983, 2002, 2003) — signals to the audience that these events are rooted in documented fact.

This epic span puts the play in company with Brechtian epic theatre structure, in which scenes function as separate episodes each carrying their own meaning, rather than as links in a single causal chain. Brecht believed that episodic structure prevented the audience from becoming lost in emotional identification; they could stand back and witness the political argument being made. In The Great Wave, the cutting between Japan and North Korea achieves a similar effect: the audience cannot fully surrender to either storyline without being reminded that another, equally real world is running parallel to it.

A common student error is to describe the play as a family drama about Japanese grief and treat the North Korean sequences as background. This misreads the structure entirely. Turnly gives roughly equal stage time to both sides; the North Korean sequences are not backdrop but a parallel central story. The examiner’s note on this is consistent: students who analyse only the Japanese family’s storyline miss the structural argument the play is making. The cross-cutting is the meaning. What the parallel structure demands of the audience is the emotional labour of holding both experiences at once — which is precisely what the abduction has denied the characters themselves.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the transition scenes between the Japan and North Korea storylines in The Great Wave. Consider lighting, sound and the physical positioning of the performers to make each cross-cut transition meaningful for the audience. You should refer to at least two named moments of transition in the play.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full discussion of at least two named transition moments; lighting choices are concrete (lantern type, colour temperature, intensity — e.g. a cold 6200K profile wash fading to black for North Korea vs a warm 3200K Fresnel for the Japanese domestic scenes); sound design choices are specific (wave soundscape swelling, then cutting to silence, then propaganda music underscore); blocking is described precisely (performers freezing downstage left in one storyline while new scene opens upstage right); costume differentiation is described; the cumulative effect on the audience of these repeated transitions is analysed. Substantiated directorial judgement about which design choice carries the most structural weight. Secure: Two design disciplines discussed, most choices concrete, at least one named moment, generally accurate audience effect. Developing: Aware of the transitions but describes design in general terms (dark for North Korea, bright for Japan); no specific lantern type, gobo or soundscape texture; limited reference to named moments. Emerging: Lists design elements with little explanation of how they work in performance.

lessons.title: Characters: The Hashimoto Family and Their Captors

before.content_html:
A Family Divided by a Coastline

Francis Turnly’s characters in The Great Wave carry the weight of a documented historical event. They are not simply dramatic constructs — they are theatrical representations of a human situation that was real for many families along Japan’s western coast in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Understanding how to perform and design these characters requires understanding both their individual psychology and their structural function in the parallel storylines. Every character exists on at least two levels: as a human being with specific desires and fears, and as an embodiment of a political relationship between two states.

Hanako: The Anchoring Figure

Hanako is 17 when she is abducted. She is the play’s central figure but also, by design, its most constrained: the physical fact of captivity means she rarely initiates action. Her dramatic arc is internal — the slow, painful accommodation to a life she did not choose, and the question of whether accommodation equals surrender or survival. A performer playing Hanako across the play’s full timeline faces one of the most demanding tasks in the GCSE set-play canon: communicating 24 years of interior change through vocal interpretation and physical evolution, without the luxury of a narrator explaining the psychological shifts.

In the early captivity scenes, a performer might play Hanako with a fast, shallow breath pattern — higher pitch, clipped phrasing, physical restlessness. She paces: she is young, frightened, disoriented. A decade later, the same performer must communicate containment without defeat. A slower pace of speech, longer pauses before responding to her captors, a more upright but very still posture — the body has learned economy, not submission. The key performance challenge is distinguishing accommodation from defeat; Hanako survives precisely because she internalises rather than breaks.

Key Fact

Hanako is the play’s emotional centre across two decades. A performer must track her ageing through specific vocal and physical changes rather than relying on costume or make-up alone: pace of speech, range of movement, and the quality of stillness are the primary tools.

Reiko: The Advocate

Reiko is Hanako’s older sister, and the last person to see Hanako before the abduction. Her arc is the inverse of Hanako’s: where Hanako is confined and controlled, Reiko becomes increasingly active, increasingly public. She refuses the easy conclusion — that Hanako drowned — and her refusal drives the Japanese storyline. A performer playing Reiko must chart a different kind of psychological journey: from grief-stricken teenager to determined adult campaigner, without losing the underlying guilt of their last argument.

In the early scenes, Reiko’s physicality might be collapsed, withdrawn, directed downward — the proxemics of grief. A performer might keep her consistently downstage right, nearer the audience but turned slightly away from the other family members — present but unreachable. In the later scenes, her energy redirects into forward motion and direct eye contact: she stands upstage centre and addresses other characters (or, in moments of direct appeal, the audience itself) with a sustained, level gaze. The posture opens, the volume increases, the pacing quickens when bureaucratic silence is confronted.

Etsuko: The Mother

Etsuko, the mother, undergoes the most visible ageing across the play. She begins as an anxious parent in middle age and ends as an elderly woman whose grief has become the shape of her life. For a costume designer, Etsuko presents an opportunity to communicate temporal change through fabric and silhouette: a domestic, practical mid-layer in the early scenes — apron, layered cottons, a dark headscarf — might give way, scene by scene, to heavier, darker fabrics that seem to weigh the body down. Hair and make-up contribute here: progressively lighter powder, more drawn lines around the eyes, slower application of movement.

For a lighting designer, Etsuko’s scenes in Japan offer the opportunity to use a warm but increasingly low-intensity lighting wash to suggest domestic space becoming emotionally colder over time. The colour temperature of the Japan sequences might shift imperceptibly from amber to a neutral white over the course of the play — so subtle that the audience feels the change before they can name it.

A common performance error for Etsuko is to play her as uniformly sad from the start. This flattens the arc. In the early scenes, Etsuko may be partly in denial — performing domestic normality — which means a performer might actually increase the pace and volume of her housekeeping activities, her insistence on routine, as a defence against grief. The breaks in this routine — the moments she stops mid-task and simply stands still — carry the greater emotional weight precisely because the activity around them has been lively. A Stanislavskian approach to Etsuko means identifying her given circumstances precisely for each scene: where is she in the emotional timeline? What does she still believe at this point? What has she been told? Has she yet seen the government’s documentation? Each answer changes what the body and voice do.

Kum-Chol and the Question of the Captor

Kum-Chol is the North Korean officer who oversees Hanako’s captivity. He is one of the most demanding characters in the play to perform because Turnly resists making him simply a villain. He is complicit in a state crime, but he is also recognisably human: he has loyalties, beliefs and, perhaps, moments of doubt. A performer playing Kum-Chol must avoid the trap of playing ideological certainty as blankness. The most interesting choices for this character involve gestus — the specific way his body communicates his relationship to institutional authority. He stands a particular way when reading official orders; he moves differently when alone with Hanako. These physical contrasts are where performance becomes analysis.

Jung Sun and the Teaching Scenes

Jung Sun is a North Korean assigned to learn Japanese from Hanako. The relationship that develops between them is the play’s most nuanced portrayal of what coercion does to human bonds. He is not free either — both of them are in the grip of the same state machinery — but his situation is different. For a director, the teaching scenes are among the most choreographically rich in the play: two people sitting across a table, both pretending a neutrality neither feels, in a space that is simultaneously a classroom and a prison. The proxemics here carry enormous weight. A director might begin with the performers at maximum downstage distance from each other and have them gradually, scene by scene, reduce that distance — a physical narrative of reluctant trust.

Key Fact

The play’s character relationships are built on constrained proximity: nearly every significant pairing is between people in unequal power positions. Proxemics — the distance between performers and whether it changes — is the most direct way to communicate these power dynamics in staging.

Examiners note that students frequently describe Hanako as ‘sad’ or ‘broken’ throughout the play and treat this as a sufficient performance analysis. It is not. The specific vocal and physical journey from frightened teenager to quietly resilient adult requires different, concrete choices at different points in the timeline. ‘Sad’ is an emotion; examiners want to know how you would embody it: lowered volume, longer inhalations before speaking, a reduced gestural range, avoidance of direct eye contact with authority figures. And crucially, these choices must change across the timeline — not because Hanako becomes happy, but because her psychological strategy evolves. A student who tracks this evolution scene by scene, with specific choices, is writing at the highest level.

What is meant by the term 'documentary theatre'?

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer could use colour temperature to communicate the contrast between Japan and North Korea in The Great Wave. Refer to specific design choices and their effect on the audience.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly's decision to root The Great Wave in the documented DPRK abduction programme shapes the audience's experience of the play. Refer to one specific staging or performance choice that draws on this context.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the play's documentary roots (the real DPRK abductions, 1977-1983) (1); analysis of how audience knowledge of these events changes the theatrical experience (1); reference to a specific staging or performance choice, e.g. the minimal institutional set of the interrogation scenes, the precision of historical dates signalled through design (1); explanation of the effect this creates for the audience (1).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Turnly uses the historical context of the DPRK abduction programme and the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration to communicate a political argument about the relationship between state power and individual life. Consider how a director might use staging to make this argument vivid for a contemporary audience.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Demonstrates specific knowledge of the historical context (abductions 1977-1983, Megumi Yokota, Pyongyang Declaration 2002); analyses Turnly's intention as using documented history to make an argument in the present tense about state accountability; discusses at least two concrete directorial choices that use historical context, e.g. the minimal institutional set signalling real bureaucratic systems, the sound design using diegetic North Korean propaganda music rooted in documented recordings, the staging of the Declaration scene as confirmation rather than resolution; explains the effect of each choice on a contemporary audience; reaches a substantiated judgement about what political argument the historical context allows Turnly to make. Secure: Demonstrates sound historical knowledge and links it to staging choices; generally concrete, at least one named moment, generally accurate audience effect. Developing: Describes the historical situation but does not connect it to specific staging choices; staging references are generic. Emerging: Brief mention of North Korea and Japan with little historical specificity or staging analysis.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would stage the scene in which the Hashimoto family learns of the Pyongyang Declaration. Consider how the staging should communicate both the significance of the official acknowledgement and the incompleteness of its resolution. Refer to lighting, sound, performer choices and proxemics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A full discussion of a specific, historicised staging of the Declaration scene. Lighting: the scene might begin in the domestic amber of the Japan sequences, then shift — at the moment of the announcement — to a cooler, more neutral state that neither celebrates nor mourns, held in an ambiguous middle register; this choice communicates that what the family has received is not a happy ending. Sound: the announcement might arrive via a radio (diegetic sound) whose volume is controlled by the performer; a soundscape that includes distant sea waves throughout the scene roots the moment in the play's controlling metaphor. Performer choices: Reiko receives the news with a controlled, quiet voice — a reduced volume that communicates shock rather than relief; her body stills completely, hands visible to the audience. Etsuko might move toward Reiko but stop at arm's length — a proxemic choice that communicates two people unable to fully comfort each other because what they have confirmed is not return, only evidence. Proxemics: the family arranged in a triangle downstage, facing toward the audience at an angle that gives the audience access to all three faces. Effect on audience: the staging communicates that confirmation is not reunion — the historical incompleteness is made emotionally immediate. Secure: Two or three strong choices, mostly concrete, at least one named design element, generally accurate effect. Developing: Aware of the emotional weight of the scene but staging is generic; limited historical specificity. Emerging: Describes what happens in the scene rather than analysing how it would be staged.

before.content_html:
A Play Rooted in Documented Events

Understanding The Great Wave as political theatre requires knowing the history it is built on. Between 1977 and 1983, North Korean agents abducted Japanese citizens from coastal communities along Japan’s western shore. The Japanese government has officially confirmed 17 cases; campaigning organisations and some academics put the number higher. These citizens were taken to North Korea and used as language teachers — teaching Japanese to North Korean operatives — and as identity sources for undercover agents operating abroad. The operation was a documented function of state policy, not an aberration.

The most widely known case is that of Megumi Yokota, who was 13 years old when she was abducted in 1977. Her case became the public face of the abduction issue in Japan and internationally: her parents spent decades campaigning for her return, and her story was documented in books, films and parliamentary hearings before and after the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration. The Great Wave is not a biographical account of Megumi Yokota or any single individual, but its research roots in these documented cases are central to how the play functions theatrically. When a director stages the abduction scene, they are staging something the audience knows — or should know — was real. This is the basic condition of documentary theatre: the audience’s knowledge of the real events is part of the theatrical experience.

Key Fact

Between 1977 and 1983, North Korea abducted at least 17 Japanese citizens (Japanese government count) for use as language teachers and identity sources. The 2002 Pyongyang Declaration was the first official acknowledgement that these abductions had taken place.

Cold War East Asia: The Political Context

The abductions took place within a specific Cold War geopolitical context. North Korea in the late 1970s and early 1980s was a tightly closed state with no diplomatic relations with Japan, operating under the leadership of Kim Il-sung. Japan, an American ally with a functioning democracy and a rapidly expanding economy, was the regional contrast: open, prosperous, constitutionally pacifist. The Sea of Japan — the body of water that separates the two countries — was the border through which the abductions were conducted, using small, fast boats on dark nights near isolated beaches.

For a set designer, the political geography of the play can be communicated through the stage itself. A traverse or traverse configuration might represent the two countries as occupying opposite ends of the stage, with the sea — the border — as the acting space between them. A director working in this configuration would be making a staging argument: that the two worlds of the play are literally separated by water, and that every cross-cut transition is a crossing of that divide. A thrust stage might bring the Japanese family sequences close to the audience, making their grief immediate, while the North Korean sequences are played at the farthest reach of the stage.

Japan in the 1980s and 1990s: The Domestic Context

The Japanese family sequences of The Great Wave take place against a backdrop of significant social change. Japan in the 1980s was at the height of its economic miracle; by the 1990s it was entering a period of economic stagnation. The families of the abductees spent these decades campaigning in a Japan that did not always want to hear about the abductions — official relations with North Korea were diplomatically awkward, and the Japanese government’s response to the abduction cases was slow and, many families felt, inadequate. A costume designer staging the Japanese family scenes might use the distinctive civilian clothing of 1980s and 1990s Japan — subdued professional wear, practical domestic layers — to ground the audience in the specific social world of families living alongside an unresolved national trauma.

The contrast with the North Korean sequences is a design opportunity. If Japan is warm, domestic and textured — layers of fabric, ambient household sounds, the soft pool of a domestic lamp — then North Korea can be its visual opposite: a world of institutional uniformity, flat surfaces, and the cold geometry of controlled space. A lighting colour palette that reserves amber and warm white for Japan and uses cool blue or neutral white for North Korea is a simple, legible visual grammar that reinforces the play’s structural argument every time a scene changes.

In September 2002, North Korean leader Kim Jong-il met Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi in Pyongyang and acknowledged that North Korean operatives had abducted Japanese citizens. Five surviving abductees were permitted to return to Japan; others, including Megumi Yokota, were declared dead by North Korea. Her family and the Japanese government contested this. The Pyongyang Declaration was a rare moment of official acknowledgement that the abductions had occurred, but it resolved almost nothing for most families. In the play, this event is a structural hinge: it is the moment the audience has been waiting for, and Turnly stages the family’s receipt of this information as a dramatic climax whose resolution is partial at best. A director staging this scene must resist the temptation to treat it as a happy ending: what the Declaration gives the family is confirmation, not return.

Francis Turnly and the Playwright’s Context

Francis Turnly is a Northern Irish playwright of Japanese-Irish heritage. His grandfather was Japanese. He lived in Japan, speaks Japanese, and spent years researching the abduction cases and meeting families affected by them. The Great Wave is his most significant work and premiered at the Tricycle Theatre (now the Kiln Theatre) in Kilburn, north London, in 2018 under the artistic direction of Indhu Rubasingham, before transferring to the National Theatre’s Dorfman stage in the same year. The Tricycle/Kiln Theatre has a long association with political documentary theatre — producing work that holds institutions to account through theatrical investigation — and this context shapes the production values and staging conventions that Turnly writes within.

For students, the playwright’s dual heritage and personal connection to Japan matter because they explain the emotional register of the play. Turnly is not a journalist reporting on a foreign case; he is a playwright with personal ties to the culture he is writing about. This gives the play a quality of given circumstances-level specificity — the domestic details of Japanese family life, the precise cultural weight of certain kinds of silence, the specific texture of grief across decades — that a more distanced political play might lack.

Key Fact

The play premiered at the Tricycle (Kiln) Theatre, Kilburn, 2018, directed by Indhu Rubasingham, transferring to the National Theatre’s Dorfman. The Tricycle’s documentary theatre tradition shapes the production’s staging conventions: factual precision, minimal theatrical artifice, the audience as witness.

Examiners note that students who treat The Great Wave as a family drama loosely set during political events miss the central analytical opportunity. The play’s documentary roots are not background: they are the reason the staging choices carry the weight they do. When a director signals the Pyongyang Declaration through a change in lighting state and the sound of a radio broadcast, the audience’s knowledge that this event actually happened amplifies the emotional impact beyond anything a purely fictional story could achieve. A student who answers context questions by describing ‘the difficult political situation between Japan and North Korea’ without naming the abductions, Megumi Yokota or the 2002 Declaration is unlikely to reach the highest marks. Specific historical knowledge, correctly applied to a discussion of staging or performance, is what distinguishes the strongest answers.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The play is rooted in the documented DPRK abduction of at least 17 Japanese citizens between 1977 and 1983; Megumi Yokota’s case is the most publicly known. The 2002 Pyongyang Declaration was the first official acknowledgement that the abductions occurred.
  • Francis Turnly’s Japanese-Irish heritage and years of research with affected families give the play a cultural specificity that distinguishes it from more distanced political theatre; it premiered at the Tricycle/Kiln Theatre in 2018 under Indhu Rubasingham.
  • Context is not background in documentary theatre — the audience’s knowledge of the real events amplifies every staging choice; design contrasts between Japan (warm, domestic) and North Korea (cold, institutional) make the political geography of the play legible and emotionally immediate.

lessons.title: Dramatic Methods: Cross-Cutting and Stage Directions

before.content_html:
Two Countries, One Stage

Francis Turnly’s The Great Wave takes place across two countries and 24 years. To hold those two worlds simultaneously, Turnly relies on a single structural engine: cross-cutting. Scenes in Japan and North Korea alternate in quick succession, so the audience is never allowed to settle entirely into one world before the other pulls them back. This is not accidental restlessness — it is Turnly’s way of insisting that both lives are happening at the same time, that Hanako’s captivity and her family’s grief are not separate stories but a single wound.

Key Fact

Cross-cutting in The Great Wave creates parallel time: the audience watches Hanako adapting to life in North Korea at exactly the same moment that Reiko and Etsuko in Japan are refusing to accept she is dead. The two timelines are always in tension.

Stage Directions and the Sea

Turnly’s stage directions do far more than describe the set. They specify the sound of the sea as a recurring presence — waves are not decorative background noise but a reminder of the beach where Hanako disappeared. A director staging the play must decide how to realise this: a soundscape of waves can fade in and out to mark every transition between storylines, functioning as an audible signal that the two worlds are connected by that same sea. The stage direction does not merely set the scene — it instructs the entire company about the play’s emotional geography.

For a designer, realising the sea means a choice between approaches. A lighting wash of shifting blue-grey across the cyclorama can evoke the sea’s restlessness without requiring literal scenic waves. Some productions have used gobos to throw fragmented light patterns suggesting water moving across the floor — so even the North Korean compound scenes carry a visual trace of the sea the captive cannot reach.

Because the play spans 1979 to 2003, transitions between scenes must carry not just geographical shift (Japan to North Korea) but also temporal shift — sometimes several years pass in a single cut. Turnly’s stage directions use a combination of signals: a change in lighting state, a costume change visible to the audience, and a change in the physical bearing of the performers. A character who was upright and defiant in the preceding scene may enter the next one carrying the weight of another two years in their posture and pace.

For the director and designer this means agreeing a consistent vocabulary for transitions. If a blackout followed by a surge of wave sound means “time has passed,” that convention must be established early and held consistently — otherwise the audience loses its bearings across the play’s long arc. The blocking at the start of each new scene can itself signal time: a performer moving quickly to a new position suggests arrival in a new moment, while stillness as the lights rise signals that this scene begins mid-thought.

Code-Switching and Language as Subtext

One of Turnly’s most striking dramatic methods is the use of language as a marker of identity and coercion. In the North Korean scenes, English stands in for Japanese (the language Hanako speaks at home and later teaches) and stylised Korean signals that she is now living inside a system that wants to erase who she is. This code-switching is a form of subtext: every time Hanako speaks in the language she has been forced to learn, the audience feels the cost of her survival.

For a performer playing Hanako, the challenge is to carry the weight of that language shift in the body as well as the voice. A shift to Korean might be accompanied by a slight change in posture — a contained stillness, proxemics that keep her at a formal distance from the officials around her — so that the audience reads the language change as a kind of performance within performance, Hanako surviving by playing a role.

Key Fact

The play’s documentary realism roots — Turnly’s years of research with abductee families — shape the dramatic methods. The stage directions specify moments of bureaucratic procedure (interrogations, declarations, diplomatic meetings) with a precision that signals: this really happened to real people. That weight sits underneath every theatrical choice.

The Wave as Structural Metaphor

The play’s title is not set dressing. A wave is something that cannot be stopped once it begins; it moves people without asking permission; it appears to recede but leaves a changed landscape behind. Turnly uses this image structurally: the cross-cutting itself moves like a wave — rising in intensity as diplomatic events accelerate in the play’s second half, and finally cresting in the scenes around the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration. A director staging the play needs to feel and shape this rhythmic architecture, using the pace of scene transitions to build that wave towards its final breaking point.

Students sometimes describe cross-cutting as though it were simply a way to “keep the story moving.” Examiners reward much more than this. Cross-cutting in The Great Wave is a political act: by refusing to let the audience follow only Hanako’s story or only the family’s story, Turnly forces us to hold both in mind simultaneously — to feel the injustice of the gap between a family waiting for news and a daughter alive but unreachable. The technique creates dramatic irony and moral pressure on the audience, not just narrative variety.

When you discuss cross-cutting in an extended-response question, always explain its effect on the audience’s emotions and understanding, not just its technical description. Ask yourself: what does the audience know in this scene that the characters on stage do not? How does that knowledge create tension or grief?

lessons.title: Staging and Design: Sea, State Apartment and Searchlight

before.content_html:
Two Worlds on One Stage

The design challenge of The Great Wave is fundamental: how do you put Japan and North Korea on the same stage without either location feeling vague? Turnly’s play demands a design language that can differentiate between two politically and emotionally distinct worlds, often within the same scene transition. The solution most productions reach for is not naturalistic scene-painting but a split staging strategy: a stage divided so that the Japanese household and the North Korean compound can each claim a permanent location, with lighting doing the work of telling the audience where they are.

For a staging configuration, an end-on or thrust stage both offer advantages for this play. A thrust configuration brings the audience close to both worlds simultaneously, collapsing any comfortable distance between spectator and the injustice they are watching — a Brechtian effect even in a predominantly naturalistic production.

Key Fact

The two locations demand contrasting design vocabularies: Japan evokes domestic warmth and coastal openness — natural light, timber, the blue-grey of the sea. North Korea evokes state control — flat, harsh overhead light, institutional walls, the absence of the natural world. Every design choice should be readable as belonging to one or the other.

Lighting Design: From Coastal Softness to State Searchlight

The Japan scenes can be lit with a warm amber-tinted lighting wash that evokes domestic interior light and coastal afternoon. For the North Korean compound, the design logic shifts entirely. A harsh overhead rig — profile lanterns angled steeply downward, producing sharp shadows — communicates institutional control without a single piece of dialogue. Hanako is surveilled; the light does not flatter or warm, it locates and exposes.

The “searchlight” image referred to in the play’s design history extends this logic: a tight lighting special that picks out a performer centre stage, surrounded by darkness, functions as both interrogation lighting and a visual metaphor for isolation. A gobo patterned with a window-frame or horizontal bars, projected across Hanako’s body, makes her captivity legible without any set-piece prison construction.

A common student error is to write: “I would use cold blue lighting for the North Korea scenes to show it is cold and unfriendly.” Examiners need much more than this. Specify: which lantern type (profile spots for hard-edged shadows; Fresnels for a softer, more diffused chill), what intensity (70% rather than full, so the actors are readable but the environment feels leached of warmth), what colour gel (a Lee 201 “Full C.T. Blue” or similar cold wash), and what directional angle (steep top-light creates institutional surveillance rather than the enveloping cold of a side or front wash). Each specific choice carries meaning; a generic description carries none.

Sound Design: Waves and Propaganda

The play’s soundscape moves between two very different audio environments. The Japan scenes carry the sound of the sea — waves that begin as natural beach noise and gradually, across the play, become something the family has to choose to hear or not. A sound designer might position the sea sound binaurally (from the sides of the auditorium) in early scenes, then bring it to a mono centre speaker in later scenes, as if the sea has retreated into memory.

The North Korean compound scenes can be underscored by institutional sound — a low, steady drone that belongs to the building, not to nature; or, more specifically, by occasional fragments of state propaganda broadcast — distant music, an announcer’s voice — that arrive not as dramatic set-pieces but as background texture, as ordinary as traffic. This is the sound of a system that does not need to shout because it is simply the air you breathe. A soundscape underscore of this kind is more unsettling than a dramatic sound cue precisely because it feels unremarkable.

Key Fact

The sea functions as a controlling sound motif: it begins the play (the beach storm where Hanako disappears) and it is always available to the sound designer as a marker of the original loss. In the North Korean scenes, the absence of the sea — or its replacement by state sound — measures how far Hanako has been taken from herself.

Set Design: Minimalism Across Decades

Because the play covers 24 years and two countries, a realistic naturalistic set would require constant scene changes and would slow the play’s momentum fatally. Turnly’s play calls for a minimalist set: a stage that holds both locations simultaneously, with a handful of key elements that can be rearranged or relit to signal transitions. A low platform levels structure can separate the domestic Japanese household at one depth from the clinical compound surfaces at another, without a scene change.

Projections on the cyclorama can carry the sea without requiring a physical construction: a rolling ocean image projected behind the Japan scenes gives way to a blank institutional wall in the North Korean compound sequences. This also allows the projection to evolve — the sea becoming stormier or calmer — in response to the emotional arc of the family’s scenes.

Costume: Decade, Culture, Coercion

Costume in The Great Wave carries enormous narrative load because it must show the passage of decades (1979 to 2003) and the erasure of Hanako’s Japanese identity within the North Korean state. The design must signal two things simultaneously: the historical period (1980s Japanese civilian clothing moves through decades) and the institutional pressure on identity (Hanako’s costume in North Korea becoming less her own over time — more muted, more uniform, less personal).

For the Japanese family scenes, costume colour and silhouette can reflect period fashion while also tracking emotional states: Etsuko’s palette might grow greyer as the years pass, her costume gradually losing the bright accent colours of the early scenes. For Hanako in captivity, a DPRK-inflected institutional grey or khaki — plain fabric, functional cut — replaces the personal clothing of the beach scene. The contrast between what she wore at 17 and what she wears a decade later can be read by the audience as the visual measure of what she has lost.

Design choices only work if the performer engages with them. A performer playing Hanako in the compound scenes can use proxemics to reinforce the costume’s meaning: keeping a formal, controlled distance from officials, never allowing her body to claim the space as her own — the body contained within the uniform rather than inhabiting it. When Hanako has a rare private moment, a small physical release — dropping the shoulders, letting the hands open — can signal the self that still exists underneath the institutional costume. These micro-choices are what separate a performance that merely wears the costume from one that lives in it.

glossary_terms.definition: A staging approach where two distinct locations are represented simultaneously on stage, often separated by light or level.
The overall shape and configuration of a performance space: how stage and audience are arranged relative to each other.
A stage that extends into the audience on three sides, with spectators on three sides and the backstage on the fourth.
A broad wash of light covering the whole stage area, often used to create atmosphere or suggest an environment rather than illuminate specific actors.
A single focused lantern used to illuminate one specific area or performer, creating contrast against the darker surrounding stage.
A metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern of light onto the stage — used here to suggest a window frame, bars, or fragmented light.
A layered design of sound — recorded or live — that creates the atmosphere of a place or moment, using multiple audio elements simultaneously.
Music or sound played quietly beneath dialogue or action to support the emotional atmosphere without drawing attention to itself.
An approach to set design that uses as few pieces of furniture and scenery as possible, creating location through light, sound and performer action rather than literal construction.
The use of different heights on stage — platforms, rostra, ramps — to create visual interest, signal status, or differentiate locations.
A large curved or flat screen at the back of the stage, used for projected images or as a background for lighting.
The physical and spatial relationship between two performers on stage, used to communicate status, emotional connection, or threat.

lessons.title: Performance Interpretation: Hanako Across Twenty Years

before.content_html:
The Challenge of Playing Time

A performer playing Hanako in The Great Wave faces one of the most demanding tasks in any of the nine set plays: she must show a journey from a defiant 17-year-old arguing on a storm-swept beach in 1979 to a woman in her late thirties who has survived captivity, forced re-education, and the slow erosion of her original self. She does this without the aid of sophisticated prosthetics or years of naturalistic preparation — she does it through the precision of vocal and physical choices, scene by scene, across the play’s 24-year arc.

This is not simply about playing “older.” Playing older is a surface effect (slowed movement, deeper voice). What the play requires is something more specific: tracking how Hanako’s relationship to proxemics, to space, to silence, changes as she learns to survive inside a system designed to contain her. The body that moves freely and claims space on the beach is not the same body ten years into captivity. The difference is not just age — it is accommodation.

Key Fact

Playing Hanako across time requires a performer to track three layers simultaneously: age (physical changes in posture, pace, breath); accommodation (how the body learns to move within a system of surveillance); and internal resistance (the private moments where the self underneath the performance emerges). All three must be visible at different moments of the play.

Hanako: Physical Containment and Release

In the beach scene — Hanako’s first appearance and her last moment of freedom — a performer can play her in full ownership of her body: wide stance, blocking that cuts across the stage diagonally, gestures that reach outward. The argument with Reiko in the storm can use full vocal range — high pitch on challenge, fast pace as the argument escalates, volume that competes with the implied sound of the wind. This is a young woman who has not yet learned that her body can be owned by someone else.

The contrast in the first captivity scenes should be stark. Now, the performer might begin reducing the size of every gesture: arms held closer to the body, movements that do not claim more space than strictly necessary, eye-contact that is carefully managed — not downcast (that would signal defeat too early) but controlled, the eye-contact of someone learning when it is safe to look and when it is not. The voice becomes more contained: lower register, measured pace, pauses that are not emotional hesitation but strategic hesitation — calculating what to say rather than feeling unable to say it.

The “release moments” — private scenes where Hanako is not under official observation — give the performer the opportunity to show what is still alive underneath the accommodation. A sudden small physical release (letting the hands open, a brief change in spine alignment) can communicate volumes. These moments should be very short — the accommodation has become second nature, the release is a flash — and they function as a kind of dramatic punctuation, reminding the audience that Hanako is not the role the state has written for her.

The interrogation scenes are some of the play’s most demanding. Hanako is being asked to confirm or deny an identity — to accept a new name, a new history. A performer who plays these scenes by trying to “look scared” misses the point entirely. The more interesting and more truthful choice is stillness: absolute stillness, placed centre stage under a harsh overhead light, with the minimum of facial expression. This choice tells the audience that Hanako is conserving herself — spending as little energy as possible, giving as little as possible, preserving something inside that the system cannot reach.

Vocally, the same principle applies. A flat, even delivery in the interrogation scenes — not dead, but carefully neutral — communicates the same conservation of self. The voice is not the character’s private voice; it is the voice produced for the officials. The distinction between this voice and the rare private voice (warmer, perhaps slightly faster) is something the audience begins to read as the play goes on, so that a shift in vocal register becomes a signal of private self re-emerging.

Reiko: Grief That Does Not Resolve

The performer playing Reiko faces a different temporal challenge: not the gradual accommodation of captivity but the gradual hardening of unresolved grief into something that looks like certainty. Reiko spends the play refusing to accept that Hanako is dead. In the early scenes this refusal is raw — it can be played with a vocal tension that sits high in the chest, a physical restlessness, hands that cannot settle. In the middle scenes, the grief has been lived with long enough that it has taken on structure — it has become a project, an advocacy position. The proxemic patterns change: Reiko moves toward people, demanding to be taken seriously, whereas early-grief Reiko might move away, closing off.

For a performer, the key is never to play the same version of Reiko twice. Each scene must show the accumulation of years. A simple physical marker — the way she holds herself when addressing officials, a very slight brittleness in the voice that was not there at the beginning — communicates the weight of two decades without requiring the performer to play every moment at full emotional intensity.

Etsuko: Resignation That Is Not Defeat

The mother, Etsuko, ages the most visibly of the three central women across the play’s timeline. But the danger in playing her is to reduce her ageing to physical signifiers only (slower movement, quieter voice) without tracking her interior journey. Etsuko’s trajectory is from active maternal grief to something that examiners often describe as “resignation” — but a performer who plays resignation as a collapse misses the point. Etsuko’s silence in the later scenes is not weakness; it is the outcome of having waited so long that the waiting has become her identity. A performer might express this through very deliberate, economical physicality — each movement purposeful, nothing wasted — and a vocal quality that is low and steady, suggesting not defeat but endurance.

Key Fact

All three central performers must show change over time: this is the play’s deepest requirement. Not a single fixed characterisation but a performance in which the audience can feel the weight of 24 years accumulating in the body and voice. Examiners reward answers that track specific changes — not just “she becomes sadder” but “in the early scenes her voice is in the upper register with rapid pace; by the final act the pace is slower and the pitch lower, suggesting the energy of grief has become the quiet weight of endurance.”

A very common performance-interpretation error is to reduce Hanako’s 24-year journey to a single emotional note: sadness, or alternatively resilience. Both are too simple. Hanako’s journey includes defiance, survival, accommodation, moments of real connection (with Jung Sun), moments of private resistance, and eventually the confirmation that her family has known she was alive — a discovery that is not straightforwardly joyful. A performer who has made a specific, evolving set of physical and vocal choices throughout the play will be able to land that final complexity in a way that a performer playing a single emotion cannot. “I would play her as sad” scores at Developing. “In the teaching scenes I would allow a small warmth to enter the voice when addressing Jung Sun — a slightly raised pitch, a fractionally faster pace — as the only moment where the accommodation shows a crack in its surface” scores at Mastering.

lessons.title: Practitioner Application: Documentary Theatre and Brecht

before.content_html:
A Play Between Two Traditions

Any production of The Great Wave must make a fundamental directorial decision: how much does it lean into its documentary theatre roots, and how much does it employ Brechtian distance? These are not mutually exclusive — in practice, the most powerful productions of the play hold both simultaneously. But understanding each tradition separately helps a director and designer make deliberate, informed choices rather than accidental ones.

Francis Turnly spent years researching the DPRK abductions and speaking with families of victims. This research heritage means that the play carries what documentary theatre scholars call an ethical obligation to the real: the events depicted happened to identifiable people. At the same time, Turnly is a dramatist, not a journalist, and The Great Wave is not a verbatim play. It uses the tools of dramatic art — composite characters, shaped scenes, theatrical climax — to communicate the truth of the abductions in a way that a simple documentary record cannot.

Key Fact

Documentary theatre (including verbatim theatre at its purest) uses the actual words, documents, or testimonies of real people. The Great Wave is not verbatim — Turnly has shaped and fictionalised — but its documentary roots give it the weight of the real: examiners reward students who understand that the play engages with documented historical events (the DPRK abductions, the 2002 Pyongyang Declaration) rather than treating it as pure fiction.

Brecht: The Audience as Witness

Bertolt Brecht’s approach to political theatre rested on a fundamental conviction: audiences who are lost in emotional identification with characters on stage are not thinking. He developed a range of techniques designed to interrupt this identification and return the audience to critical awareness. His term for the distancing effect produced by these techniques was the Verfremdungseffekt, often translated as the “alienation effect” or “estrangement effect.”

For The Great Wave, the Brechtian frame is powerful because the play is about a political crime: the DPRK abductions are not a private tragedy but a state act, and Turnly wants the audience to understand them as such. A director who applies Brechtian thinking might use direct address at key structural moments — a scene might pause, a character might step out of the fiction to address the audience as though they are witnesses rather than spectators. Projected titles (dates, locations, the number of confirmed abductees) can interrupt scenes to insist that this is not just a story but a documented event.

Brecht’s concept of gestus is directly applicable to the power dynamics of The Great Wave. The officials who oversee Hanako’s captivity can be staged with a gestus that makes their social role unmistakable: a particular upright bearing, a way of occupying the stage that signals authority without requiring it to be stated. Kum-Chol, the North Korean officer, is a character Turnly renders as recognisably human — but a Brechtian directorial choice might use gestus to ensure the audience always reads the role he plays in the system, even in his most sympathetic moments.

While Brechtian techniques work powerfully for the play’s political argument, the role of Hanako cannot be reduced to a gestus. Her 24-year journey demands what Stanislavski’s method offers: a detailed understanding of the character’s given circumstances (what has been taken from her, what she still has), her objectives at each moment (to survive, to preserve herself, to find some form of connection), and her relationship to the other characters as real psychological encounters rather than symbolic positions.

The teaching scenes with Jung Sun are the clearest example. These scenes depend on the audience sensing a genuine emotional shift in Hanako — something approaching warmth, however provisional — even within captivity. A Brechtian approach alone would flatten this. Stanislavski’s attention to given circumstances (what does Hanako know, what does she need, what is the emotional history between these two people?) gives the performer the tools to make that warmth specific and earned. The result is a production that can be politically clear (Brechtian) and emotionally true (Stanislavskian) at the same time.

The Ethical Dimension: Staging Real Victims

Because The Great Wave is based on real people’s experiences, any production carries an ethical responsibility that a fully invented play does not. A Brechtian directorial approach can honour this: rather than asking the audience to live through Hanako’s captivity as a fully immersive emotional experience (which would place us in the centre of her story), the Brechtian frame positions us as witnesses. We are asked to see clearly, to think, to judge — and perhaps to act. This is the didactic intent of political theatre: not to make audiences cry and go home, but to make them understand something they could choose to act on.

Key Fact

The most successful productions of The Great Wave use both practitioners: Stanislavski for the private emotional truth of Hanako and the family (so the audience cares); Brecht for the political frame (so the audience thinks and understands the systemic cause). The two approaches do not cancel each other out — they produce the complexity the play requires.

The Hashimoto Household: Where Documentary Meets Domestic

The Japan scenes — the Hashimoto family (referred to in early scenes and staging materials as this) — offer a design and performance zone where the documentary and domestic meet. The design can be naturalistic enough to feel real (a Japanese domestic interior, period detail from the 1980s onwards) while the blocking and spatial arrangement reflect the Brechtian idea that every domestic arrangement is also a political one: who sits at the table, who stands, who approaches the officials. A tableau at a key moment — the family receiving news from the officials, frozen in the light — can function as both a Brechtian quotation mark (“look at this image”) and a moment of Stanislavskian emotional weight.

Many students believe that applying Brecht means the audience must not feel anything — that emotional engagement is the enemy of political thinking. This is a misreading of Brecht’s own practice. Brecht wanted audiences to feel; he wanted them to not be incapacitated by feeling. His techniques interrupt total identification at key moments — they do not prohibit warmth, sympathy or even grief. In The Great Wave, a production that generates no emotional response to Hanako’s situation will fail to communicate why the abductions are an injustice worth caring about. The Brechtian frame asks the audience to understand the systemic cause of their emotional response — not to switch it off.

practice_questions.text: Name the Northern Irish playwright who wrote The Great Wave.
What is gestus in Brechtian theatre?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying gestus as a performance technique involving a physical pose or attitude; 1 mark for explaining that it expresses the social relationship between characters at a given moment, making the power dynamic between them immediately readable to the audience.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a director could use one Brechtian technique to communicate the political dimension of The Great Wave to the audience. Refer to a specific moment in the play.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming a Brechtian technique (direct address, projected titles, gestus, tableau, Verfremdungseffekt; 1); explaining how it would be applied to a specific moment of the play (e.g. projected date and location titles at each scene change to insist this is a documented event; 1); effect on the audience (positions them as witnesses to a political crime rather than spectators of a domestic drama; 1); link to Turnly’s intention (the play is about a real state act, not just individual suffering; 1).

practice_questions.text: As a performer playing Kum-Chol, the North Korean officer who oversees Hanako's captivity, explain how you would use vocal and physical choices to show that he is both complicit in the state system and recognisably human. Refer to at least one vocal and one physical choice and explain the effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response holds both dimensions simultaneously. Physical choices that signal systemic authority (upright bearing, formal proxemics, a gestus of institutional belonging — e.g. a particular way of standing in a doorway that signals ownership of the space) alongside physical choices that reveal humanity (a moment of stillness when listening to Hanako that suggests something other than pure official engagement; a fractionally longer pause before an order). Vocal choices similarly: a formal, even register for official transactions, but a shift in tone or pace in private exchanges. The response anchors these to named moments and explains the effect on the audience: they are held in a dual response, understanding him as a perpetrator and as a person, which is the play’s moral complexity.

Secure: at least one specific vocal and one physical choice; named moment; effect on audience present; some engagement with the dual character.

Developing: describes what Kum-Chol is feeling without translating into specific choices; or plays only one dimension (either evil or sympathetic, not both).

Emerging: generic emotional description; no specific choices; no named moment.

practice_questions.text: As a lighting or sound designer, explain how you could use design choices to reinforce the Brechtian political frame of The Great Wave. Refer to at least one specific design choice and its effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: the response proposes design choices that function as Brechtian devices — projected titles (dates, number of abductees, location) in a plain sans-serif typeface on the cyclorama at key transitions (interrupting the naturalistic fiction to insist on documentary reality); or a cold, high-contrast lighting state for the official scenes that makes them feel less naturalistic than the family scenes (a design “estrangement”); or a sound design that introduces institutional broadcast sound without the emotional preparation a naturalistic production would use (no gradual fade-in, just the sound arriving — a Brechtian shock cut). Every choice is named specifically (e.g. projected white sans-serif text at 80% opacity on the cyclorama; or a sudden cut to tinny propaganda audio at mid-volume from a single downstage speaker) and the effect on the audience is stated: the audience is reminded that this is a documented event, not a private story.

Secure: at least two specific design choices; at least one linked to Brechtian technique; effect on audience present.

Developing: general design ideas (“I would use cold lighting”) without linking to Brechtian technique or naming specific elements.

Emerging: describes the desired atmosphere without specific design choices; no link to practitioner.

practice_questions.text: You are directing The Great Wave. Discuss how you would apply both Brechtian techniques and Stanislavski's approach to different moments of the production to serve the play's dual purpose: political argument and emotional truth. Refer to specific moments of the play and specific staging choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: a clear directorial vision is articulated that uses both practitioners purposefully. Brechtian choices: direct address at the official announcement scenes (audience positioned as jury); gestus for the officials and Kum-Chol (making their social role legible); projected title cards at scene transitions (insisting on documentary reality); a design language for the North Korean compound that is slightly less naturalistic than the Japan scenes (harder edges, less texture, more institutional geometry). Stanislavskian choices: detailed given circumstances for Hanako’s arc (what she has lost, what she still has, what she wants from each encounter); specific vocal and physical choices for the teaching scenes with Jung Sun (warmth, however provisional); the emotional truth of Etsuko’s waiting given full interior life. The response explains why each practitioner is appropriate to which type of scene and shows awareness that the two approaches reinforce rather than contradict each other. Named moments throughout. Audience effect throughout.

Secure: both practitioners addressed with at least one specific application each; named moments; effect on audience present.

Developing: one practitioner addressed in detail, the other mentioned but not applied; general choices.

Emerging: describes what the practitioners believed without applying their techniques to the play; no named moments.
